title: One object or two?
intro: A String variable holds an arrow to a String object. Literals live in the string pool and are shared; `new` always builds a fresh object. And no String ever changes: a method that seems to change one builds a new one.

rounds.right: Three variables, two objects: the pool shares a literal, and `new` refuses to.

why.b: A literal that is already in the pool is reused: `b` gets an arrow to the very object `a` points at.
why.c: `new String(...)` always builds a fresh object outside the pool, even though the pool already holds the same text.

rounds.right: `==` compares arrows and `equals` compares text: same text in two objects is `equals`, but not `==`.

why.a==b: `a` and `b` were made from the same literal, so the pool gave them one object: `==` compares the arrows, and they end at the same place.
why.a==c: `==` compares arrows, not text: `c` points at the object `new` built, a different one from `a`'s.
why.equals: `equals` compares the text, character by character, and the text is the same in both objects.

rounds.right: Catch the arrow: `s = s.toUpperCase();` keeps the new String. Without the `s =`, it is built and thrown away.

why.uncaught: `toUpperCase()` can't change the String `s` points at: Strings never change. It builds a new one and returns it, and this line throws the result away.
why.caught: This time the result is caught: `s = ...` moves `s`'s arrow to the new upper-case String.

rounds.right: Sharing a String is always safe: `a` moved to a new object, and the one `b` points at can never change.

why.alias: `a + {suffix}` builds a new String and only `a`'s arrow moves to it. `b` still points at the original, and nothing can change that object.
why.a==b: After the `+`, `a` points at the new String and `b` at the old one: two arrows, two objects.
